lead: The highest microwave powers still come from electrons flying through vacuum. A microwave tube makes a DC electron beam hand its kinetic energy to an RF field. The klystron amplifies by bunching the beam in cavities, the reflex klystron oscillates by turning its beam back through one cavity, the magnetron oscillates at high power in crossed fields, and the travelling-wave tube (TWT) amplifies over a wide band along a helix. Radar, satellite links, accelerators and microwave ovens use them.
prereq: You need: cavity resonators (see Microwave resonators and Q factor) and ½mv² = eV.

sections.h3: Two-cavity klystron: velocity modulation and bunching

blocks.text: A gun forms a beam of current I₀ accelerated through V₀, so electrons enter at v₀ = √(2eV₀/m) = 0.593 × 10⁶ √V₀ m/s. The beam crosses the input cavity (buncher) gap, where the RF input sets up V₁ sin ωt.

Take as reference the electron that crosses when the gap voltage is zero and rising. Earlier electrons met a retarding field and leave slower; later ones meet an accelerating field and leave faster. In the drift space the fast late electrons catch up with the slow early ones, and the beam gathers into one bunch per RF cycle: velocity modulation becomes current modulation.
v(t) = v₀[1 + (β<sub>i</sub>V₁/2V₀) sin ωt],   X = (β<sub>i</sub>V₁/2V₀) θ₀,   θ₀ = ωL/v₀
blocks.where: β<sub>i</sub> = sin(θ<sub>g</sub>/2)/(θ<sub>g</sub>/2) is the beam coupling coefficient of a gap of transit angle θ<sub>g</sub> = ωd/v₀ (d = gap width); θ₀ is the drift transit angle over the drift length L; X is the bunching parameter.

blocks.text: The fundamental RF current of the bunched beam is 2I₀J₁(X), largest at X = 1.841, where J₁ = 0.582. The bunches cross the output cavity (catcher) gap while its field retards them and give it energy. The efficiency is η = β₀V₂J₁(X)/V₀ for an output gap voltage V₂, so it is at most J₁(1.841) = 58.2 % when β₀V₂ ≈ V₀; real tubes give less. Multicavity klystrons add idle cavities to sharpen the bunches and raise the gain.

sections.h3: Reflex klystron: one cavity and a repeller

blocks.text: A reflex klystron is an oscillator. The beam crosses one cavity and meets a repeller at −V<sub>R</sub> with respect to the cathode. The retarding field (V<sub>R</sub> + V₀)/L sends the electrons back through the same gap, bunched by the round trip; if the bunches return while the gap field opposes them, they feed the cavity and oscillation builds up.
ωT′ = 2πN,   N = n + ¾ (n = 0, 1, 2 …);   V₀/(V<sub>R</sub> + V₀)² = (2πN)² e / (8ω²L²m)
blocks.where: T′ is the round-trip time, N the mode number (¾, 1¾, 2¾ …), V<sub>R</sub> the repeller voltage magnitude and L the repeller distance.

blocks.text: Each mode has its own repeller voltage, and only modes with V<sub>R</sub> > 0 exist. Small changes of V<sub>R</sub> pull the frequency within a mode (electronic tuning); a tuning screw changing the cavity moves the centre frequency (mechanical tuning). The best efficiency of a mode is 2X′J₁(X′)/(2πN) with X′ = 2.408: 22.7 % in the 1¾ mode. Output is milliwatts; it served as a radar local oscillator and bench source.

A cylindrical magnetron has a cathode of radius a inside an anode of radius b cut into N cavities. V₀ gives a radial electric field and a magnet an axial field B₀. With no RF, electrons curve back before reaching the anode when B₀ exceeds the Hull cutoff field (or V₀ is below the Hull cutoff voltage).
B₀c = √(8V₀m/e) / [b(1 − a²/b²)],   V₀c = (e/8m) B₀² b² (1 − a²/b²)²,   f<sub>c</sub> = eB₀/(2πm) ≈ 28 GHz × B₀
blocks.where: B₀c in tesla, V₀c in volts, a and b in metres; f<sub>c</sub> is the cyclotron frequency with B₀ in tesla.

blocks.text: Above cutoff the electrons form a rotating space-charge wheel whose spokes keep step with the RF field across the cavity gaps. In the π-mode the phase step between cavities is 2πn/N with n = N/2, so neighbours are 180° apart; straps on alternate vanes keep the tube in it. Magnetrons give megawatt pulses at 40 % to 70 % efficiency, but each pulse starts with a random phase.

A TWT has no resonant cavity. A wire helix slows the RF wave to the beam speed: the wave follows the turns at nearly c, so its axial velocity is about c × p/(2πa) for pitch p and radius a. With the beam slightly faster, electrons bunch and feed the wave all along the helix. The helix is not resonant, so one tube covers an octave or more. Its gain is

blocks.where: C is the gain parameter, Z₀ the helix impedance, I₀ and V₀ the beam current and voltage, and N the helix length in electronic wavelengths.

examples.question: A two-cavity klystron has V₀ = 1200 V, I₀ = 30 mA, f = 4 GHz, gap width d = 1 mm and drift length L = 3 cm. Find v₀, the gap coupling coefficient, the drift transit angle, the input gap voltage V₁ for maximum bunching, and the maximum efficiency.
steps: ω = 2π × 4 × 10⁹ = 2.513 × 10¹⁰ rad/s. Gap angle θ<sub>g</sub> = ωd/v₀ = 2.513 × 10¹⁰ × 10⁻³/2.054 × 10⁷ = 1.223 rad.
Drift angle θ₀ = ωL/v₀ = 2.513 × 10¹⁰ × 0.03/2.054 × 10⁷ = 36.70 rad (5.84 cycles).
Maximum bunching at X = 1.841: V₁ = 2V₀X/(β<sub>i</sub>θ₀) = 2 × 1200 × 1.841/(0.939 × 36.70) = 128.2 V.
Beam RF current 2I₀J₁(1.841) = 2 × 30 × 0.582 = 34.9 mA; maximum efficiency 58.2 % of V₀I₀ = 36 W, so at most about 21 W of RF.
examples.answer: v₀ = 2.05 × 10⁷ m/s, β<sub>i</sub> = 0.939, θ₀ = 36.7 rad, V₁ = 128.2 V for X = 1.841, and at most 58.2 % (about 21 W of the 36 W input).

examples.question: A reflex klystron has V₀ = 600 V and a repeller distance L = 2 mm, and oscillates at 8 GHz. Find the repeller voltage for each possible mode, and the round-trip time in the 1¾ mode.
steps: From V₀/(V<sub>R</sub> + V₀)² = (2πN)²e/(8ω²L²m): V<sub>R</sub> + V₀ = √(8ω²L²V₀m/e)/(2πN). Here √(8 × (5.027 × 10¹⁰)² × (0.002)² × 600/1.759 × 10¹¹) = 16 608 V, so V<sub>R</sub> + V₀ = 16 608/(2πN) = 2643.3/N volts.
For N = 1.75: V<sub>R</sub> + V₀ = 1510.5 V, so V<sub>R</sub> = 910.5 V (repeller at −910.5 V with respect to the cathode).
N = 4.75 needs V<sub>R</sub> = −43.5 V, a repeller above cathode potential, which cannot return the beam: only four modes exist.
examples.answer: Repeller voltages 2924 V, 910.5 V, 361 V and 105 V for the ¾, 1¾, 2¾ and 3¾ modes; T′ = 0.219 ns in the 1¾ mode.

traps: Getting the bunching backwards. Fast electrons start behind the slow ones and catch up.
Using N = n for a reflex klystron mode. The bunch must return ¾ of a cycle late, so N = n + ¾ (¾, 1¾, 2¾ …).
Reading π-mode as a frequency. It means adjacent magnetron cavities oscillate 180° apart.
Mixing units in efficiency. kV × mA gives watts directly; converting only one gives an error of 10³.

quiz.q: What is the job of the drift space in a two-cavity klystron?
quiz.a: It gives the faster electrons time to catch the slower ones, so the velocity modulation from the input gap becomes current bunches at the output gap.

quiz.q: State the oscillation condition of a reflex klystron.
quiz.a: The round-trip time in the repeller space must be (n + ¾) RF periods: ωT′ = 2π(n + ¾), n = 0, 1, 2 …

quiz.q: Why is a TWT broadband while a klystron is narrowband?
quiz.a: A klystron couples through resonant cavities, which work only near resonance. A TWT uses a non-resonant helix whose wave speed matches the beam over a wide frequency range.

quiz.q: A cylindrical magnetron has a = 5 mm, b = 10 mm, V₀ = 20 kV and B₀ = 0.3 T. Find the Hull cutoff field, the Hull cutoff voltage at 0.3 T and the cyclotron frequency. Will electrons reach the anode with no RF?
A helix TWT has V₀ = 2.5 kV, I₀ = 20 mA, Z₀ = 20 Ω and N = 40. Find C and the power gain.
A reflex klystron gives no output until its repeller voltage is changed slightly. Explain.
quiz.a: The bunch must return (n + ¾) cycles after leaving. At a wrong V<sub>R</sub> the bunches return in an accelerating field and take energy from the cavity, so oscillation dies. Changing V<sub>R</sub> changes the return time and brings the tube into a mode.

quiz.q: Compare a magnetron and a TWT as the transmitter of a pulsed radar.
quiz.a: A magnetron is a cheap, efficient oscillator giving megawatt pulses, but narrowband, with random phase from pulse to pulse, which prevents coherent Doppler processing. A TWT is a broadband amplifier of lower peak power that amplifies a stable coded waveform coherently. Magnetron for simple high-power radar; TWT where bandwidth or coherence matters.

beyond: Gyrotrons use cyclotron motion in a strong magnetic field to reach megawatts at millimetre waves for fusion heating. Space TWTs with depressed collectors still power many satellite downlinks. Search for "gyrotron", "depressed collector" and "coupled-cavity TWT".

figure.caption: The beam picks up velocity modulation in the input cavity, bunches while drifting, and gives up energy in the output cavity; the collector takes the spent beam.
